theory.intro: A chord or arc **subtends** an angle at a point when both its endpoints are joined to that point. The angle may be at the **centre** or at the **circumference**. The arc on the far side from the vertex is the arc it **stands on**.
facts: A chord or arc **subtends** an angle at a point when both endpoints are joined to that point.
Different points on the circumference each subtend their own angle on the same chord, and vertices on one arc all stand on the other.
steps: Identify the two endpoints of the chord or arc that forms the base of the angle.
Identify the vertex — the centre $O$, or a point on the circumference.
Join the vertex to both endpoints, and name the angle with the vertex as the middle letter.
To name the arc an angle stands on, find the arc between the two endpoints that does not contain the vertex.

foundation.solution_text:
The chord $PQ$ is joined to the centre $O$.
The angle at the centre subtended by $PQ$ is $\angle POQ$.

The chord $PQ$ is joined to the circumference point $R$.
The angle at the circumference subtended by $PQ$ at $R$ is $\angle PRQ$.

$\angle XOY$ is formed by joining $X$ and $Y$ to the centre.
The chord that subtends this angle is $XY$.

foundation.question_text: What word describes the relationship between a chord (or an arc) and the angle it forms when its two endpoints are joined to another point?
foundation.solution_text:
Joining the two ends of a chord or arc to a point forms an angle at that point.
The chord or arc is said to **subtend** that angle.

$\angle AOB$ has its vertex at $O$, the centre, so it is the angle at the centre subtended by $AB$.
$\angle ACB$ has its vertex at $C$, a circumference point, so it is the angle at the circumference subtended by $AB$.

Joining $A$ and $B$ to $C$ gives $\angle ACB$.
Joining $A$ and $B$ to $D$ gives $\angle ADB$.
$\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ both stand on the same arc $AB$.

$\angle XZY$ is formed by joining $X$ and $Y$ to the circumference point $Z$.
The chord that subtends this angle is $XY$.

development.solution_text:
$P$ and $Q$ are joined to the circumference point $R$ (not the labelled point $S$, which plays no part here).
The angle at the circumference subtended by $PQ$ at $R$ is $\angle PRQ$.

$X$ lies on the long way round from $Y$ to $Z$, so $X$ is on the major arc $YZ$.
An angle stands on the arc that does not contain its own vertex, so $\angle YXZ$ stands on the minor arc $YZ$ — the short arc between $Y$ and $Z$.

$R$ lies on the short way round from $P$ to $Q$, so $R$ is on the minor arc $PQ$.
An angle stands on the arc that does not contain its own vertex, so $\angle PRQ$ stands on the major arc $PQ$ — the long arc between $P$ and $Q$.

Angle $1$ has vertex $O$, the centre, with arms to $A$ and $B$ — this is the angle at the centre subtended by $AB$.
Angle $2$ has vertex $C$, a circumference point, so it is the angle at the circumference subtended by $AB$, not the centre.
Angle $3$ has vertex $A$, an endpoint of the chord itself, so it is not subtended by $AB$ at all.
The answer is angle $1$.

The vertex of the angle is $Z$, the point where its two arms meet.
In angle notation, the vertex is always the middle letter.
Ben is correct: $\angle XZY$ has $Z$ as the middle letter, matching the vertex; Priya's $\angle ZXY$ puts the vertex first, which names a different angle (with vertex $X$).

The angle at the centre subtended by $AB$ is $\angle AOB$.
$C$ and $D$ both lie on the circumference, so the angles at the circumference subtended by $AB$ are $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$.

$\angle XOY$ is formed by joining $X$ and $Y$ to the centre, so the chord that subtends it is $XY$.
The minor arc $XY$ (the shorter arc between $X$ and $Y$) subtends this same angle at the centre.

mastery.solution_text:
a. $A$ and $C$ are joined to the centre, so this is $\angle AOC$.
b. $B$ is on the major arc, so this is $\angle ABC$.
c. $D$ is on the minor arc, so this is $\angle ADC$.
d. $\angle BOD$ is formed by joining $B$ and $D$ to the centre, so the chord it subtends is $BD$.

a. $E$ and $G$ are joined to the centre $O$, so the angle at the centre subtended by $EG$ is $\angle EOG$.
b. $E$ and $G$ are joined to the circumference point $F$, so the angle at the circumference subtended by $EG$ at $F$ is $\angle EFG$.
c. $\angle OEF$ has its vertex at $E$, one of the chord's own endpoints, not at a separate point joined to both $E$ and $G$.
An angle subtended by $EG$ must be seen from a third point with both $E$ and $G$ as its arms' endpoints, so $\angle OEF$ does not fit this and is not subtended by $EG$.

a. $H$ and $I$ are joined to the centre, so this is $\angle HOI$.
b. $J$ and $K$ are joined to $H$ and $I$, giving $\angle HJI$ and $\angle HKI$.
c. Since $J$ and $K$ both lie on the major arc, the arc not containing either vertex is the minor arc — $\angle HJI$ and $\angle HKI$ both stand on the minor arc $HI$.
